newsitem.title: UK: UK's PIA pensions regulator forms enforcement unit.
newsitem.headline: UK's PIA pensions regulator forms enforcement unit.

text.p: Britain's Personal Investment Authority (PIA), which regulates the sale of pensions and other investments to the public, said on Monday it had formed a new enforcement division to strengthen its investigative hand.
The PIA is currently under close scrutiny as a controversial inquiry into pensions mis-selling by some financial firms drags into its third year.

Will Hastings, PIA spokesman, told Reuters that the 60-strong unit, formed from investigators from its member relations division and litigation experts taken from its legal division, would make it more effective in this task.
"The PIA believes that the reorganisation will ensure that it is able to deal with investigations and any subsequent disciplinary action in a highly-efficient manner," he said.
Pension mis-selling has affected several hundred thousand people who may have been wrongly advised to take out personal pensions by advisors during the late 1980s and early 1990s.

Criticism of the regulators' slow progress has taken in both the PIA, as the "frontline" regulator which independently authorises firms to conduct their business, and the Securities and Investment Board (SIB) which supervises the system of rules.

In particular, critics have pointed at the seemingly slow rate of completion of the review and at the way some companies being pursued for compensation have dragged their heels. Last week SIB chairman Sir Andrew Large surprised observers by deciding to give up his post at the end of May. He picked out the unsatisfactory rate of progress on the pensions mis-selling review as the main piece of unfinished business on his agenda.
Sources in the insurance industry recently told Reuters the PIA appeared to be stepping up pressure on insurers to resolve outstanding cases by chasing up some of the worst offenders.
They said the PIA had held a series of meetings with firms with a large number of cases yet to be settled to get them to outline their plans to clear up the backlog.

Last week Britain's largest insurer, Prudential Corp Plc said it had reached agreement with the GMB trade union to compensate some of its members and end litigation in the courts over alleged mis-selling.
The new enforcement division will be headed by Stuart Willey, previously head of the PIA's legal services team.
